faq.a: Their periventricular white matter contains immature oligodendrocytes that are highly sensitive to low oxygen and inflammatory cytokines.
faq.q: Why are preterm infants especially vulnerable to PVL?

faq.a: Optimising maternal health, preventing preterm birth, treating chorioamnionitis, and using gentle ventilation strategies reduce risk.
Mild cases may have normal cognition with motor therapy; severe PVL often leads to spastic diplegic cerebral palsy and learning difficulties.

exam: A 28‑week preterm infant shows increasing head size and hypotonia at 3 weeks – what is your next step? — Perform cranial ultrasound; if cystic lesions are seen, diagnose PVL and arrange neuro‑rehab.
How does chorioamnionitis contribute to PVL pathogenesis? — It triggers fetal inflammatory response, releasing cytokines that damage pre‑myelinating oligodendrocytes.
Explain why a normal bedside ultrasound does not exclude PVL. — Ultrasound detects only cystic lesions; diffuse white‑matter injury may be invisible, requiring MRI or clinical follow‑up.
Which motor pattern distinguishes PVL‑related cerebral palsy from peripheral neuropathy? — Spastic diplegia with preserved reflexes and upper‑limb strength points to central white‑matter injury.

What neuro‑protective measures are recommended for a preterm infant at risk of PVL? — Antenatal steroids, delayed cord clamping, gentle ventilation, and maintaining normothermia reduce ischemic injury.
Why are high‑dose phenobarbital seizures discouraged in PVL infants? — Phenobarbital can worsen neuro‑developmental outcomes; newer agents (e.g., levetiracetam) are preferred when available.
List three rehabilitation strategies for a child diagnosed with PVL. — Early physiotherapy for tone management, occupational therapy for hand function, and speech therapy for language delays.

In a low‑resource setting without MRI, how would you monitor progression of PVL? — Serial head circumference, regular neuro‑developmental exams, and repeat cranial ultrasound if cystic changes appear.
ai.title: Periventricular Leukomalacia
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) is a form of white‑matter brain injury in preterm infants caused by ischemia‑reperfusion and inflammation. It leads to motor and cognitive deficits that may evolve over months. Early recognition guides neuro‑protective care and parental counseling.

b: Clinical picture may be silent at birth, evolving over weeks
sections.p: PVL is the most common cause of cerebral palsy in very low‑birth‑weight infants. The injury occurs in the periventricular white matter, where oligodendrocyte precursors are vulnerable to hypoxia, infection and oxidative stress.

b: Cystic PVL: echogenic lesions that evolve into cysts on ultrasound
Diffuse PVL: subtle signal change on MRI, often missed without advanced imaging
sections.p: Understanding PVL requires linking perinatal risk factors, the pathophysiology of white‑matter injury, and the neuro‑developmental sequelae that guide follow‑up.

b: Early hypotonia progressing to spastic diplegia
Poor head‑control, delayed sitting, asymmetric hand use
Seizures may occur in severe cases
sections.p: PVL presents with evolving motor tone abnormalities, delayed milestones, and visual‑motor deficits. In low‑resource settings, limited imaging makes bedside assessment crucial.
